newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin meets EU leaders at start of critical week.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin meets EU leaders at start of critical week.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, making a further step in his political comeback after illness, met a European Union delegation at the Kremlin on Monday at the start of a week that could bring a big government shake-up.
Opening talks with Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok and European Commission President Jacques Santer, the 66-year-old leader said he was pleased with the state of Russian-EU relations.
The Netherlands holds the EU's rotating presidency.
"I'm very glad that a pretty good dialogue is getting under way between us and the EU and its leadership," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying as the talks got under way.

Following the discussions, the Kremlin press office said in a statement that the president had repeated Moscow's bitter opposition to plans to admit former Soviet-bloc states in eastern Europe to the West's NATO defence alliance.

Apparently trying to engage the support of the EU, whose expansion plans Russia finds less threatening than those of the U.S.-led military pact, the Kremlin said the meeting noted "the efforts of Russia and the European Union, in the interests of a united Europe free from lines of division".
The Kremlin described Russian-EU relations as "key to strengthening security and stability on the continent".
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana visits Moscow this weekend in a new bid to soothe Russian objections to expansion.
The Kremlin statement said a previously agreed partnership and cooperation accord, designed to forge commercial links and to liberalise trade, would come into effect before the summer.
It added that agreement was reached in principle on a permanent mechanism to deal with economic, trade, scientific and cultural issues between Russia and the EU.

The Russian side pressed its claim for more access to European markets -- something EU companies fear could unleash a flood of cheap imports. Russian trade with the EU is already up to 10 times greater than with the United States.
The Kremlin statement said Kok and Santer pledged to help Moscow integrate into the world economy. Brussels wants to push Russia to prepare for admission to the World Trade Organisation.

Yeltsin's EU summit was originally scheduled for February 4 in The Hague but had to be postponed when the president came down with pneumonia in January after a brief return to the Kremlin following his November heart bypass operation.

Clearly determined to stamp his authority on subordinates and opponents after spending the first eight months of his second term out of action, Yeltsin has sharply criticised Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's budget and demanded a reshuffle.

Government changes are expected to be announced after Yeltsin faces his biggest physical test in public since his re-election campaign when he gives a 40-minute state of the nation address in parliament on Thursday morning.
Some media have speculated Chernomyrdin himself could go but many analysts say the 58-year-old, a touchstone of stability for foreign investors during his four years in office, will stay on.
"B.N. Yeltsin stressed that policies of democratisation and deepening of economic reforms will not change," the Kremlin said in its statement on the EU summit.

Deputy Communist party leader Valentin Kuptsov told the party's Central Committee that patience with the government was running out and it could face a no-confidence motion next month in the opposition-dominated State Duma lower house.
Kuptsov said Chernomyrdin had reneged on promises to pay out wage and pension arrears which he had made in order to secure communist backing for the government's 1997 budget.
"There could be an expression of no confidence in the government if these conditions are not met by March 31 or concrete measures to fulfil them are not presented," he said.
Under Russia's constitution, parliament has little practical power to oust the government appointed by the president.
